The Paris Office, announced in March 2026 and to
be located at the World Bank Group’s Paris office,
will support training activities and strengthen
connections with State officials, legal practitioners, and
organizations in the region and beyond. Paris has long
been one of the Centre’s most active hearing venues.
In fiscal 2026, 30 percent of all in-person hearings were
held at the World Bank Group Paris Conference Centre,
ICSID’s premier hearing venue in use since 1972, and
at facilities of leading institutions with which ICSID has
established cooperation agreements.
Together, these offices reflect ICSID’s commitment to
bringing its services closer to Member States, parties,
and practitioners.
SHARING KNOWLEDGE, SUPPORTING
PRACTITIONERS AND POLICYMAKERS
As part of the Knowledge Bank, ICSID produces and
shares knowledge that actively contributes to the
development and modernization of international
investment law and dispute settlement.

Of all
the in-person hearings in fiscal 2026, 44 percent were
held at ICSID’s hearing center in Washington, D.C., with
the remainder taking place at venues agreed upon by
the parties: Paris (30 percent), London (12 percent),
Singapore (5 percent), and other locations (9 percent).
ICSID continued to see a diverse pool of arbitrators,
conciliators, and committee members in fiscal 2026.
The Centre recorded 250 appointments to ICSID
cases, the second highest number in a single fiscal
year. Appointees represented 52 different nationalities,
and 29 percent of all appointments were nationals from
low- or middle-income economies. First-time appointees
accounted for 8 percent of all appointments; among
them, 25 percent were nationals of low- or middleincome economies and 35 percent were women.
The ICSID Secretariat comprises 76 staff members representing 39 nationalities and
speaking 22 languages, providing professional legal, administrative, and financial
services across all cases.

EXPANDING GLOBAL PRESENCE

and expanding its global presence is among its current
institutional priorities. Fiscal 2026 marked a landmark
moment in this effort with the announcement of new
offices in Singapore and Paris, the Centre’s first staffed
offices outside Washington, D.C. This expansion will
enhance ICSID’s capacity to deliver tailored support,
strengthen outreach, and maintain the highest
standards in case management.
The Singapore office, announced in August 2025, is
located at the World Bank Group’s Singapore office and
at Maxwell Chambers. It will serve as a regional hub
for capacity building in investment dispute settlement;

MEMBERSHIP UPDATES AND BENEFITS
REACHING FURTHER, WORKING CLOSER
ICSID continued to deepen its worldwide engagement
in fiscal 2026. Staff participated in over 180 activities,
the most in a single year to date, across 60 cities as part
of a robust outreach and capacity-building program.
Delivered in person and remotely in the Centre’s
three official languages (English, Spanish, and French),
as well as in Italian and Japanese, these activities
reached officials from over 90 States, along with legal
practitioners, students, and representatives of regional
and local institutions.

Each case is assigned a dedicated management team led
by an experienced legal counsel and supported by paralegals and legal assistants. A
finance and administration team oversees the financial aspects of cases and manages
the planning and logistics of ICSID sessions and hearings, while an institutional
matters team handles ICSID membership and the Centre’s publication program.

participated in five sessions of the United Nations

State-led reform discussions, including by submitting
comments on the feasibility of modifying the ICSID

permanent appellate tribunal. ICSID also deepened
its engagement with the International Institute for the
Unification of Private Law (UNIDROIT) in support of
efforts to modernize and harmonize investor-State
investment contracts.

As a cooperative institution, IBRD does not seek to
maximize profit but rather to earn enough income to
ensure the long-term financial capacity necessary to
sustain its development activities. Allocable net income
in fiscal 2026 was $2.3 billion, and out of this, the
Executive Directors approved the allocation of
$1.1 billion to the General Reserve, and recommended
to the Board of Governors an allocation of $750 million
to IDA and $500 million to Surplus. Further, the Board
recommended to IBRD’s Board of Governors the
following transfers out of Surplus: $300 million to the
IBRD Trust Fund for Gaza and West Bank, $100 million
to the Grant Facility for Project Preparation, and
$100 million to the IBRD Surplus-Funded Livable Planet
Fund. As part of its lending, borrowing, and investment
activities, IBRD is exposed to market, counterparty,
country credit, and operational risks.

In fiscal 2026, new
IBRD lending commitments amounted to $50.2 billion
for 147 operations, of which 13 were IBRD and IDA
blended operations.

MAXIMIZE DEVELOPMENT IMPACT
Shareholder support for IBRD’s innovative financing
instruments continued to grow in fiscal 2026,
strengthening our capacity to scale lending and tackle
global challenges. Singapore pledged funds to our
hybrid capital instrument and New Zealand became
the first shareholder to subscribe to our Enhanced
Callable Capital instrument, bringing hybrid capital
contributions to $1.2 billion. Together, these new
instruments demonstrate IBRD’s strong leveraging
power, turning $1 into $6-10 of additional lending over
time, and unlocking tens of billions for global impact.
IBRD has continued to structure outcome bonds that mobilize private capital for
specific development projects. For example, in December 2025, IBRD issued a
$200 million principal-protected bond, the Clean Cooking Outcome Bond, that
mobilized private capital to support the distribution and use of cleaner cooking
stoves in Ghana.

IBRD FINANCIAL RESOURCES

AND FINANCIAL MODEL
IBRD finances its loans through its own equity and by
borrowing in the capital markets via the issuance of
IBRD bonds to fund development projects in member
countries. IBRD is rated triple-A by both Moody’s and
Standard & Poor’s, and investors view its bonds as highquality and liquid securities. IBRD’s funding approach
continues to aim to achieve the best long-term value
for borrowing members on a sustainable basis. IBRD’s
ability to channel the funds it raises in international
capital markets to developing member countries is
important in achieving its goals.
IBRD’s approach has enabled it to borrow at favorable
market terms and pass the savings on to its borrowing
members. Funds not immediately deployed for lending
are held in IBRD’s investment portfolio to provide
liquidity for its operations. In fiscal 2026, IBRD raised
nearly $50 billion by issuing medium- and long-term
bonds in a variety of currencies.

agencies and other international organizations to

results.text:
In fiscal 2026, ICSID published its first in-depth study on
contract-based investment dispute resolution, drawing
on an analysis of 175 cases registered under the ICSID
Convention and Additional Facility. The background
paper examines how contract-based dispute resolution
has worked in practice at ICSID, serving as both an
analytical guide and practical reference for investors,
States, and State entities. Key findings show that
contract-based arbitrations at ICSID are more timeefficient than the overall caseload, averaging 40 months
from registration to conclusion compared to 47, and
settle or discontinue at a higher rate, 43 percent versus
34 percent. The paper is accompanied by a special
issue of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics featuring data on
contract-based cases.

Two issues of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics were also
released. Published every six months in English, French,
and Spanish, this publication offers a comprehensive,
data-driven overview of all cases registered and
administered by ICSID since 1972, serving as a key
resource for practitioners and policymakers to track
trends and developments in international investment
dispute settlement.
Visit icsid.worldbank.org/resources/
publications to download and read all ICSID
publications.
CASE MANAGEMENT AND
DISPUTE RESOLUTION
ICSID administers investment disputes arising from
contracts, treaties, or laws when agreed upon by the
parties involved. Disputes are decided by an arbitral
tribunal or a conciliation commission, whose members
are typically appointed by the parties from among
international jurists worldwide. The Centre also offers
mediation and fact-finding procedures, and provides
administrative services for arbitrations conducted
under UNCITRAL and other non-ICSID frameworks.

FIGURE 5: ICSID ADMINISTERED CASES BY FISCAL YEAR
Fiscal 2026 was a record year for ICSID. The Centre
administered 363 cases — the highest in its history —
up from 347 in fiscal 2025 and 341 in fiscal 2024. In
addition, ICSID provided services in 15 cases governed
by non-ICSID rules in fiscal 2026, 12 of which were
conducted under the UNCITRAL rules.
During fiscal 2026, ICSID registered 60 new cases —
57 arbitrations under the ICSID Convention and three
under the Additional Facility Rules — bringing the
cumulative total to 1,118 registered cases as of
June 30, 2026. On the mediation front, ICSID had
received a total of seven requests under Mediation
Rule 6 and Mediation Rule 5, with one proceeding
administered as of fiscal 2026. The year also saw 83
proceedings concluded, marking the third consecutive
fiscal year in which conclusions surpassed 80.

Of the arbitrations concluded in fiscal 2026, 63 percent
were decided by a tribunal and 37 percent were settled
or otherwise discontinued, broadly reflecting ICSID’s
long-term trend of arbitration outcomes. Among
disputes decided by tribunals in the past year,
37 percent of awards upheld claims in part or in full,
40 percent rejected all claims on the merits, 18 percent
declined jurisdiction, and 5 percent of cases were
dismissed for manifest lack of legal merit.

domestic investment laws. ICSID’s rules and procedures
are widely regarded as the gold standard for
investment dispute settlement, offering a stable and
predictable legal framework that balances the interests
of both States and investors and has been modernized
over time to reflect best practices in the field.

investment law and dispute settlement by producing
and sharing knowledge, building capacity, and
engaging with Member States and other stakeholders
on investment dispute prevention, management,
and settlement.

tracks key development impact indicators to allow

track. In fiscal 2026, 65 percent of the 1,570 projects

impact at the end of the project’s implementation

DELIVERING MORE FOR CLIENTS
Further promoting private capital mobilization, we
helped countries refinance their outstanding IBRD
loans on now-proven projects where lending can be
considered “de-risked” from a commercial lender’s
perspective. For India, this approach unlocked nearly

which offers volume, tenor, and price incentives, to
encourage clients to undertake projects that address
global challenges with cross-border benefits. Under

benefiting from a 43-year IBRD loan, eight years
more than the current 35 years, and received

support energy sector modernization.

AND FINANCIAL MODEL

borrowing in the capital markets via the issuance of
IBRD bonds to fund development projects in member
countries. IBRD is rated triple-A by both Moody’s and

continues to aim to achieve the best long-term value
for borrowing members on a sustainable basis. IBRD’s
ability to channel the funds it raises in international
capital markets to developing member countries is
important in achieving its goals.

are held in IBRD’s investment portfolio to provide
liquidity for its operations. In fiscal 2026, IBRD raised
nearly $50 billion by issuing medium- and long-term

is closely managed in line with its financial and risk

STABILITY IN PANAMA
When Panama faced serious fiscal strain in 2025, the
World Bank Group responded with an unprecedented
approach by combining IBRD and MIGA guarantees in
a jointly structured policy-based financing operation.
Building on lessons from a similar operation in Côte
d’Ivoire, teams designed a layered structure pairing
a $500 million IBRD Development Policy Loan with
$1.4 billion in commercial financing covered by
two guarantees: a $600 million IBRD Policy-Based
Guarantee for first-loss coverage, and a MIGA NonHonoring of Sovereign Financial Obligations guarantee
for second-loss coverage.
This approach, resulting in approximately $1.9 billion
in financing, was approved simultaneously by
both institutions’ boards, moving from approval to
disbursement in about a month.
